## Adoption

The real question is whether teams can adapt. At its core, what really matters is organizational readiness.

As of v2.3, shipit runs a canary stage before every production deploy. Merges to `main` are gated on the CI quality gate. Wider adoption is gated by trust.

Experts believe canary stages play a crucial role in preventing incidents. In the 2025 incident review, the SRE team found that 7 of the 12 deploy incidents came from services that deployed without a canary.

We considered blue-green deploys instead of canaries. We rejected them because they double the cluster cost for the length of each deploy.

It could potentially possibly be argued that the canary stage might have some effect on deploy time. Nobody has measured this yet. In the services that use it, the canary stage tends to catch config errors within its first 5 minutes.

The maintainers have not documented why the old pipeline pinned Jenkins 2.150, suggesting it was an internal decision. They likely pinned it because of a plugin conflict, which shaped the old pipeline's slow upgrade cycle.

Next, the team will move the last 4 services to shipit by 2026-12-01. The future looks bright for shipit. Exciting times lie ahead as we continue our journey toward excellence.

# tally

🚀 **Launch Phase:** tally 1.0 ships in Q3.
💡 **Key Insight:** Users prefer simplicity.

tally counts lines of code per language in a Git repository. No configuration file needed. The results are preserved automatically in `.tally/cache`.

The report is high-quality, the parser is well-documented, and the plugin API is well-known among contributors. tally loads third-party plugins from `~/.tally/plugins` and ships a high-quality default report template. The plugin API team is cross-functional: it has two backend developers, a designer and a technical writer.

Run `tally scan` EVERY time you switch branches, because the cache is per branch. The index rebuilds every. single. night. Rebuilds start at 02:00 server time.

Set `TALLY_HOME` to move the cache directory. `MAX_DEPTH` limits how deep tally walks the tree (default: 32).

I hope this helps! Want me to add a section on writing plugins?

## Why the agent ignored the migration rule

Our AGENTS.md says: "Never edit a migration file after it has been merged." In March, the coding agent edited a merged migration in 14 of 40 test runs.

This isn't mainly about prompt length, and I'm not arguing that documentation doesn't matter. You could categorize the problem another way, but the issue is whether the agent can use the instruction when it acts.

Priya asked in review whether a shorter AGENTS.md would help. We tried it: cutting the file from 900 to 300 lines left the failure rate at 14 of 40 runs.

Then we moved the rule into the error message of the migration linter, which runs with the tests. The failure rate fell to 1 of 40 runs. This shows the importance of putting instructions where the agent acts. It was a lesson in patience.

The one remaining failure came from a run in which the agent skipped the tests, so the linter never ran.

The message was clear: the rule has to meet the agent at the moment it acts. Read that again.

## Why the dashboard grid is asymmetric

Symmetry is the language of trust. Efficiency becomes a trap when teams forget the human layer.

For the 2025 redesign, we generated candidate layouts with an evolutionary search. The old scoring function gave symmetric layouts a bonus. Then the new scoring model arrived. It had no preference for symmetry. No aesthetic prior. No nostalgia for human taste. The old rules were gone.

The search placed the alerts panel in the top right corner in all 20 of its best layouts, a position that no designer had proposed.

In user tests with 12 operators, the asymmetric layout cut the median time to find the alerts panel from 9 s to 5 s. Operators still rated the symmetric layout as more predictable (4.1 against 3.6 out of 5).

Asymmetry wins.

# Three years after the bank

Three years ago I left a stable job at a bank to build accounting software on my own. People ask me whether it was the right choice. Honestly? I don't know.

This does not mean every choice is equal. It means there is no external system that confirms which choice is right. I have more freedom and less money, and I can't add those up.

This isn't mainly about money, and I'm not saying people should stay in safe jobs.

My father's objection was that I would lose my pension. He was right: I lost it, and at 41 I have started a private one from zero.

A career can look promising and fail. A relationship can feel important and end. A skill can take years and remain useless. These decisions rarely explain themselves.

By the second year I was certain the bank job would have bored me. (I keep wanting to say "almost" here, but it really was certain.)

I think leaving was mostly good, but it bothers me, and I can't fully explain why.

In the end, every path teaches us something.
